in writing. on the basis of the report by my romanian colleague, renate weber, i voted for the european parliament's legislative resolution supporting the initiative of several member states (belgium, the czech republic, estonia, spain, france, italy, luxembourg, the netherlands, austria, poland, portugal, slovenia, slovakia and sweden) to strengthen eurojust. i support the strengthening of the data protection component of the proposal and the fact that the european parliament is better informed to better control the tasks and missions of eurojust which was established in 2002 as a body of the european union with legal personality to promote and improve coordination and cooperation between the competent judicial authorities of the member states. the experience gained by eurojust shows that its operational efficiency must be enhanced, in particular by ensuring that the status of its national members is approximated. i also support the emergency coordination unit, the national coordination systems, partnerships with the other community instruments for security and protection (europol, frontex, olaf) and the possibility for eurojust to second liaison magistrates to third countries.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of the report by mrs lambert on the evaluation of the dublin system. the report rightly points out that, on the whole, the objectives of the system have been largely achieved, but that due to the lack of precise data it has not been possible to assess the cost of the system. some concerns remain, both in terms of practical application and the effectiveness of the system. the report opens the debate on the future of the european common asylum policy which was launched in june 2007 with the publication of the green paper. the report stresses that the following aspects of the system need to be clarified or modified: applicants must be given all relevant information on the dublin system in a language they understand and have access to legal aid throughout the procedure, and must have a right of appeal against any transfer decision; the criteria for determining the age of minors should be harmonised; mechanisms should be designed to freeze transfers to states that are clearly not respecting the rights of applicants.
in writing. the main purpose of this text, under the guise of strengthening eurojust's operational capacity in the fight against various forms of crime, is to satisfy the obsessive political correctness of the thought police. the objective of monitoring all speech under threat of punishment, whether written or spoken in meetings, is hardly veiled. indeed, different voices have already been raised in the european parliament in order to adopt a framework directive aimed at penalizing alleged racism and xenophobia and creating a single european prosecutor's office for its rapid transposition, that is to say a new torquemada of the union's 'political correctness'. unfortunately, the more decision-making power the european parliament, the self-proclaimed temple of democracy, acquires, the more fundamental freedoms, including the freedoms of research, opinion and expression, are trampled on. in reality, this totalitarian europe is far more dangerous than the monsters it claims to be fighting. the main aim of the supporters of the euro-globalist and immigrationist ideology is to eliminate their troublesome opponents by adopting repressive european criminal legislation. we do not accept that.
in writing. i voted for the report by my british colleague jean lambert on the 'dublin system' and welcomed the work done by the rapporteur for our epp group, my friend patrick gaubert. this mechanism aims to determine the member state responsible for examining an asylum application lodged by a third-country national in the territory of one of the eu member states, norway or iceland. while, in general, the objectives of the dublin system, including the establishment of a clear and viable mechanism for determining the member state responsible for examining an asylum application, have been largely achieved. but, beyond the unassessed cost, there are still problems with the efficiency of the system and practical applications. all of this shows the urgency of a european immigration and asylum policy and i welcome the work of the current president of the relevant council, my friend mr brice hortefeux, minister of immigration, integration, national identity and solidarity development of the french republic, who has just chaired the european ministerial conference on asylum law in paris on 8 and 9 september 2008.
in writing. i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on the own-initiative report by my british colleague sharon bowles on a coordinated strategy to improve the fight against tax fraud, in response to a commission communication on the same subject. tax revenue, i.e. the total amount of compulsory taxes and social contributions, represented 39.3% of gdp in the european union in 2004, or €4.1 trillion. very few estimates are available as to the extent of uncollected taxes due to tax evasion, which is estimated to be around 2 to 2.5% of gdp. while taxation is a matter of national competence, tax evasion constitutes an obstacle to the proper functioning of the internal market in so far as it leads to distortions of competition between taxpayers. it is clear that the fight against tax evasion has a european dimension, particularly at international level, through the phenomenon of economic globalisation.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mrs bowles' report is typical of this house: it proposes solutions to problems which would not exist without brussels europe, solutions which would only aggravate these problems or create new ones. in this case, the solutions proposed to combat tax evasion consist in demanding taxation in the country of origin, with the creation of a clearing house which would make the tax revenues of the states dependent on transfers made by the other member states. the commission has also proposed that vat be charged at the rate of the importing member state (instead of the current exemption) or that the mechanism of self-liquidation be applied. if this were to be accepted, it would result in administrative and tax headaches for businesses. in addition, direct access to computer data on taxpayers in other member states would be generalised for tax administrations. taxation of savings and criminal law for fraud would be uniformised. a number of reduced vat rates would be abolished. all this shows that the real objective is not so much to combat fraud, which is a real and worrying problem, but to put an end to the fiscal sovereignty of the member states.

the development of services are yet to be realised. it goes through the competition, but it doesn't stop there. it is a question of creating the conditions for sustainable and responsible development, in other words, an ecosystem of this knowledge economy that we all want. we must now consider ict as a resource in its own right. it is therefore a public/private issue which requires flexible regulation and accountability for all stakeholders through cooperation between regulators and the commission, as between operators and customers by contract. i have identified four pillars that i have set out to strengthen: service to the consumer, whether in terms of access through more ambitious territorial deployment fair price or quality; sustained industrial activity to ensure employment and innovation, technological progress also being a factor in lowering prices; the competitiveness of our companies, large and small, which guarantees sustainable competition in our territories and the necessary investments, particularly in fibre, to strengthen our position on the world stage; and finally, legal certainty, i.e. the reliability of the system through the accountability of the actors entity has its proper place: the commission may raise doubts about a remedy but cannot completely challenge it unless bert also issues a negative opinion. conversely, in the event of functional separation, the commission and bert must agree on both sides. in this context, this separation remains a tangible threat, but it cannot be taken lightly. as regards spectrum, our proposals are aimed and tools to encourage investment and, if necessary, to guide deployment now. as such, our proposals were validated by a panel of recognized experts just before the summer holidays. a final problem the rapporteur. - mr president, the russian foreign minister, mr lavrov, called mr kushner's "sick imagination" when he spoke of sanctions against russia. it is on this 'imagination' that i have been given to work during this report. and i would like to thank the commission and the council for being so helpful and so available. what is the debate today on sanctions? the first is the criticism of the use of punitive measures which would first of all punish the bad little ducks on the international stage, that is to say those who go against my strategic interests, politicized sanctions with double standards. the second criticism is that sanctions are not effective, mainly because they are perverse, always misused, and should therefore be done without. the aim of this report is not to advocate more sanctions or tougher sanctions or to abandon them. it is essential to look for all the conditions which make sanctions effective and the aim of this report is, indeed, to put them to rest. effective in what way? well, compared to the goal. and in the case of violations of human rights or international and humanitarian law, the aim must be to bring about a change in the behaviour of the entities concerned. this is the essential point. the sanction is neither a punishment nor the application of some kind of european penal code in international use. sanctions are a politically delicate instrument, and very demanding in its implementation, which aims to achieve a change in practices and behaviour. the eu is highly reluctant to sanction all-round, and to date has 31 sanctions regimes targeting third states or entities, mostly consisting of arms embargoes and targeted sanctions designed to have the maximum impact on the entities whose behaviour they are expected to influence, while limiting as much as possible the negative humanitarian impact. this is a rather positive observation, but i cannot say more at this stage. the eu is continuing its actions without ever producing comprehensive impact studies. we therefore have little to assess the capacity of our sanctions to resolve crises and promote human rights. the aim of this report is therefore to advocate a more transparent, more effective and therefore more credible european sanctions policy. the first essential task: to immerse oneself in an evaluation exercise. secondly, we must adopt a rigorous method, by means of preliminary studies of the specific situations requiring sanctions, in order to determine the most appropriate response to bring about change. in recent days you have been making a tour of the measures available to the union to put pressure on the russian authorities, for example. the positive aspect of the conclusions is that the stated objective is clear and can be practically assessed. it's about the six-point agreement. and in all circumstances it is essential that this be so. it is essential to include clear, precise criteria which must remain until the end, that is to say sometimes for a long time, the necessary and sufficient conditions for the lifting of sanctions. these criteria must therefore be realistic and objectively measurable. the arms embargo on china after tiananmen is perfectly legitimate, but it is not surprising that it has no positive effect, since the european union has not made its lifting conditional on any specific demand. too often, sanctions policy is approximate and flexible, depending on the political contingencies of the most influential member states or the commercial or geopolitical importance of the entities targeted. that is why, in order to give credibility to the union's policy, i am proposing the creation of a network of independent experts to assist the commission in the difficult work it is carrying out, under very difficult conditions, since it has virtually no resources to do so. let us not be mistaken. it is not a question of depriving the council of its prerogatives of political impulse or the commission of its power of proposal, but simply of offering ourselves the guarantee of an informed choice. but that's not all. punishment is a tool. it is one of the instruments - i refer you to the first two reports of the subcommittee on human rights - a comprehensive and integrated sanctions policy must be devised; there is no effective sanction without a human rights strategy in the country concerned. sanctions must be discussed at all levels and monitoring mechanisms, for example the human rights clause, must be used to the full. any sanctions against a country must always be accompanied by visible, and therefore political, but also practical, support for human rights defenders in the country. this is also a key point in the report. finally, the report also considers that any deliberate and irreversible damage to the environment is in fact a violation of human rights and therefore calls for it to be included among the grounds for sanctions. it also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the eu's financial instruments are used effectively and to ensure that the eu's financial instruments are used effectively. in short, this report attempts to respond to the present characteristics of the world crises.

reply also to mrs koppa, who has a very developed intervention, sanctions remain a political instrument. they are not the only instrument for promoting human rights. there are two other instruments member of the commission. − mr president, i think this was a very useful discussion which highlighted a number of very important issues that we have to reflect upon when we opt for sanctions, because sanctions are just one of our foreign policy tools. we always have to apply them, after careful overall reflection, in conjunction with all other tools, including development work or political and economic reform in third countries. with all these tools we want to achieve one thing: upholding and promoting human rights. mrs flautre’s report clearly shows that we need to refine this instrument further and make sure that our system of sanctions is in itself fully in line with international law, and does not violate fundamental human rights we all subscribe to. i believe that our courts – as indeed the european court of justice has done today – contribute substantially to developing our sanctions system while at the same time safeguarding fundamental principles like the rule of law and due process. again, we should promote human rights and save the wider population, not punish them, either economically or otherwise. this is very important. i shall repeat, therefore, that we must target sanctions at those responsible for human rights violations and – as mr rack said – opt for instance for freezing accounts and visa bans so as to deprive those leaders or those responsible for human rights violations of any positive possibilities. a number of speakers, indeed mrs flautre herself, have also asked for a proper evaluation of eu sanctions and have suggested the development of a certain methodology. i think jean-pierre jouyet has already briefly referred to the work done in this respect in the council, which i would like to support, and in particular i think we should improve somewhat on the ex ante evaluation before imposing sanctions. here i could also offer again the services of our delegations because they are sur place and they have a very good knowledge of what is going on; contributions by civil society and human rights organisations are certainly very useful there. with regard to coherence i would like to say that sanctions are an important tool, but they must be complemented with a proactive approach in our development work: support for human rights institutions, political reform, promoting of civil society. burma/myanmar is a good example of that. sanctions are there while, at the same time, keeping open the possibility of working with ngos and human rights organisations. i think this is one important way forward.

in writing. the general agreement on trade in services (gats), which provides for the liberalisation of services at global level and which the rapporteur is keen to see concluded, is in reality a global bolkestein directive. yesterday's "polish plumber" will be tomorrow's chinese or pakistani. the only exception is 'services provided in the exercise of governmental authority' which 'are not provided on a commercial basis or in competition with one or more suppliers'. in other words, only the police, the judiciary, the diplomatic corps and the military are not involved. on the other hand, the gats will be a further step in the dismantling of public services initiated by the commission 15 years ago in the name of competition and the internal market. the european union now believes that it can take advantage of a competitive advantage and argues that its service providers have insufficient access to third country markets. but services will be like industry: relocations and desertification, with, in addition, the import of social dumping. the report also calls for the establishment of a european network of national and regional authorities responsible for the protection of the environment.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on trade in services to invite the commission to promote, in trade negotiations, both the gradual and reciprocal opening up of access to the services market and a policy of increased transparency. the european union, the world's largest exporter and provider of services, can only encourage greater access to the services market, both at the level of developed countries and at the level of developing countries. however, this opening up must be gradual and reciprocal, taking into account the different interests of the states. in this respect, i voted in favour of amendment no 2, which recalls the need to distinguish between commercial and non-commercial services and to have a differentiated approach in opening up the markets for services of general interest. i also voted in favour of amendment no 5, which calls for universal, accessible and sustainable public services to be guaranteed for all in the context of epas. finally, in voting in favour of amendment no 7, which recognises that certain products, such as water, should be regarded as universal public goods, i wanted to point out that the opening up of the market for such services must be considered with caution.

in writing. mountain agriculture is a key issue for local economic development and environmental protection (combating climate change, biodiversity, providing safe and open recreational and tourism areas, etc.). the specific disadvantages faced by mountain farmers due to altitude, topography and climate justify the payment of compensatory allowances for natural handicaps and the receipt of direct income support to compensate them for the extra costs of production and also for the increasing role of managers of the land they occupy. in my view, the main issues are: avoiding the total decoupling of agricultural aid, particularly in the livestock sector, as this is likely to lead to job losses; helping the dairy sector, which plays a central role in disadvantaged areas; increasing support for the establishment of young farmers; and encouraging solidarity between the downstream and upstream sectors, particularly in water management. i also support the establishment of a genuine integrated european strategy for the mountains, which should be based on the integration of the specific features of the mountain ranges in the development of the various european policies.
in writing. the ebner report on the situation and prospects of agriculture in mountain regions highlights the characteristics and needs of these regions, which account for 40% of the european territory. these areas face natural difficulties which make production more difficult and limit their access. they therefore deserve special attention. i therefore call for the commission to draw up an overall plan which would be in line with the measures taken so far but would integrate them with each other in order to increase their effectiveness. the aim would be to continue to promote compensatory payments exclusively for compensation for natural handicaps, to provide financial support for young farmers and to give particular importance to the dairy sector. human activities must be maintained in the mountain areas classified as natura 2000. finally, the role of hunting and fishing in the maintenance of the spaces must be emphasized. such a strategy will enable these regions to meet the challenges of competitiveness and sustainable development, as they are not only potential sources of economic growth, but also guardians of high-quality productive traditions and help to preserve our landscapes.
i'm the reporter. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank all the colleagues who have worked with me on this dossier because our cooperation has been really excellent throughout the whole procedure. the text we are going to vote on today is a particularly sensitive text because what is meant by 'fighting terrorism' is 'threatening the rights of european citizens', whether that danger comes from the terrorists themselves or from the potentially liberticidal measures adopted to counter them. the scale of the terrorist threat has in recent years been exaggerated by some governments in an attempt to justify the adoption of security policies, both domestically and internationally. the threat is real and the european union must play its full part in the efforts to prevent and combat it with the utmost firmness. it is about the security of its 500 million inhabitants, it is about defending the fundamental values and principles on which it is founded. since the attacks of 11 september 2001, the territory of the union has also been repeatedly hit by terrorist attacks with the tragic consequences we all know: madrid in march 2004 and london in july 2005. and you all heard about the wave of attacks that took place, as of yesterday, in cantabria. the renewal and diversification of the tools and methods used by terrorists, however, makes the task much more difficult. the development of information and communication technologies, and in particular the internet, facilitates the organisation of terrorist networks and the dissemination of propaganda messages and online training manuals. it is estimated that there are now some five thousand such sites. hence the quite legitimate desire of the european commission to adapt community legislation in order to try to prevent not only terrorist attacks as such, but also the acts preparatory to such attacks. it has drawn directly from the council of europe convention on the prevention of terrorism. the problem is that it has chosen to deal only with the repressive aspects of the convention, while leaving aside the provisions on the protection of fundamental freedoms, which, according to the council of europe itself, are its indispensable counterpart. my concerns were mainly related to the concept of 'public provocation' and the risk it poses to freedom of expression, since this new charge is intended to punish words or writings that are alleged to have led to the commission of a terrorist act or are simply likely to have such an effect. at the april round table with the national parliaments we found that we were not the only ones to express reservations about certain aspects of the commission's text. several national parliaments have thus expressed doubts as to the application of this framework decision and the scope of the concept of 'public provocation'. the council of europe also highlighted the danger of the absence of safeguard clauses. finally, independent experts have expressed reservations in various studies, in particular on the definition of 'public provocation' and on the level of legal certainty of the text. the council itself, at the instigation of a handful of national delegations with a particular concern for the protection of fundamental rights, added a number of safeguards to the text of the framework decision. but it also proposed to tighten it up on one or two specific points and, in any case, work remained to be done to achieve a fully satisfactory level of legal security and protection of freedoms. we have therefore tried, together with my colleagues in the libe committee, to find the right balance between the two seemingly antinomic but fundamentally inseparable objectives of combating terrorism and protecting fundamental freedoms and rights. we have had to make a delicate balancing act, especially since it is often difficult in practice to know where freedom of expression ends and where the violation of the law begins. the scandal of danish cartoons two years ago and, more recently, the controversy of a short film on islam by dutch member of parliament geert wilders. that said, i think the compromise we have reached is a good one. the main changes we have made are as follows: first, the replacement of the term 'provocation' by the more precise and more commonly used term 'incitement' in criminal language; secondly, a stricter definition of 'public incitement' which makes it possible to define more clearly the behaviour to be criminalised and thus to avoid possible abuses which would lead to a restriction of freedom of expression; thirdly, the addition of numerous provisions in the body of the text relating to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms and, in particular, freedom of expression and freedom of the press; fourthly, the need to ensure that the measures taken are proportionate to the objective pursued, which is essential in a democratic and non-discriminatory society. that's the gist of this case. i am glad that this topic has been chosen as the priority for this morning's plenary session and i look forward to a rich and lively debate.

president of the council. - mr ryan, the question you raise is important because it concerns the effectiveness of development aid. it is important to keep a significant volume of development aid, and i will come back to that, but you are quite right in stressing in your question that this aid must be effective. in order to have effective aid, and also to be able to fight against fraud and misuse of development aid funds, there must be better coordination and complementarity between donors. that is why we are working on a joint multiannual programming based on poverty reduction strategies which make it possible to see better how funds are allocated and according to which objectives, and which also make it possible to control better the allocation of funds. this is why we have established common implementation mechanisms, including joint analyses. in particular, there are large-scale joint missions, which are funded by both donors and beneficiaries, so that there are co-financing mechanisms. these issues were on the agenda of the 3rd high level forum on aid effectiveness held in accra last week. we discussed this at the last part-session here at the beginning of this month. at the forum in accra at the beginning of september, an action plan was adopted. it corresponds to a large extent to the expectations we had for the european union. the main commitments made by donors are: to plan better, three to five years in advance, the aid that is to be provided; to use the administrations and organisations of the partner countries; to make the most of the opportunities offered by the community's external aid; to make the most of the opportunities offered by the community's external aid. the commission is also proposing to change the rules on the use of the financial instrument from those imposed by third countries to those based on objectives set by the developing countries themselves. as regards the monitoring of the delivery of assistance, both the council and the european parliament have the possibility to assess annually how the union's external assistance has been used. this evaluation is carried out by means of the annual report on the development and external aid policies of the european community and their implementation, which the commission generally presents towards the end of june - which, according to the information i have, should normally have been done last june. i would add that the development cooperation instrument provides for tools to protect the community's financial interests, particularly, as mr ryan wishes, with regard to fraud and irregularities. so there are evaluation mechanisms, control mechanisms, mechanisms to ensure better coordination between donors and beneficiaries, but ultimately the real objective will be to ensure that these policies are appropriated by the beneficiary countries, to continue to focus on good governance and to ensure that there is better accountability, particularly on the part of the beneficiaries of these aids, for the allocation of our aid. that is what i wanted to point out.

president of the council. - mr president, in reply to mr mitchell on this serious issue, the union remains very seriously concerned about the iranian nuclear programme and the lack of iranian willingness to fully address the concerns raised by a possible military dimension of this programme. in december 2007, the european council stressed that it would be unacceptable for iran to acquire a nuclear military capability. in this regard, the council has repeatedly deplored iran's failure to comply with its international obligations as set out in un security council resolutions 1696, 1737, 1747 and 1803, in particular the suspension of all its uranium enrichment activities, which is a fundamental element in order to be able to develop the necessary framework for opening negotiations and moving towards a long-term solution. the union has always affirmed iran's right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy, and if iran wishes to restore the confidence of the international community in the peaceful nature of its nuclear programme, it must suspend sensitive activities related to the nuclear fuel cycle. the proposals made by javier solana in june 2006, and reiterated in june 2008 on behalf of the six countries most closely involved, are still valid and must help us break the current impasse. the union strongly regrets that iran suspended the provisional application of the additional protocol in february 2006. the result, as the director-general of the international atomic energy agency has pointed out, has been to reduce the agency's knowledge of certain aspects of iran's nuclear programme. moreover, as the director-general of the iaea has just reiterated in his report of 15 september, iran refuses to answer the agency's specific questions on activities linked to the design and manufacture of nuclear weapons. as the director of the agency has pointed out - the commission's vice-president - mr president, i also thank all the speakers and once again our rapporteur. i would like to remind you, following what minister jean-pierre jouyet said, that we are very attentive to compliance with data protection rules. the services are in regular contact, as you have pointed out, mr minister, with the services of the european data protection supervisor to ensure the proper integration of these rules in the development and management of sis ii. a visit by the european data protection supervisor to the strasbourg site is planned for the first half of 2009, before the migration takes place, to ensure that data protection security is respected. the converter being developed will also allow for the secure transfer of data from sis 1 to sis ii. mrs lefrançois rightly said that this migration should not be rushed, and she is right. we'll have to be very careful. in addition, the legal instruments contain specific provisions to ensure compliance with the data protection principles. i can say this about data protection, knowing that we must be extremely careful to ensure that this system is consistent with what we are trying to promote in europe in terms of data protection. i'll be back in a little bit. i fully understand mr marinescu, mr lax and mrs lefrançois, who have obviously stressed the concern that has arisen from these successive delays. as far as preparations for sis ii at central level are concerned, we are following developments very closely, we have put in place means to ensure very close monitoring and the commission services are particularly keen to ensure that there are sufficient resources to monitor the work of the contractors. of course, we can use the penalties provided for in the contracts, if necessary, as my predecessor did, by imposing a penalty of more than one million euros on one of the contractors. but, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, rather than creating penalties, i want to of friends of sis ii, which was established by the slovenian presidency and confirmed by the french presidency, is extremely useful. this high-level group, in which the commission is actively involved, has the objective of monitoring the implementation of sis ii in the member states. it is only by working together that we can solve the problem. i simply want to say that we are not building a fortress europe with sis ii, we are simply making sure that the abolition of internal borders does not mean, for the european union, for the community of european citizens, an increased risk of insecurity, violence, terrorism. i cannot therefore allow you to say that by creating sis ii we are closing the doors to europe. that's not what this is about. it is simply a question of ensuring that, having abolished our internal borders, we can offer the european citizens an area - yes, i say it - an area of security and freedom. this is the president. in any case, i thank parliament and mr coehlo personally for putting so much effort into building sis ii, which is, once again, the key to the success of schengen.

in writing. the report raises the question: is it because the 'first generation' schengen system did not work or was at least ineffective in guaranteeing security within the schengen area that a 'second generation' is being developed to make up for these shortcomings? unfortunately, no. this second generation is just a more modern version of a system that is already inoperative. according to figures provided by the european commission, 400 000 illegal immigrants cross the union's borders every year. even if biometric data were soon available and usable for the registration and return of illegals already registered as illegal immigrants, the european union would be unable, in the absence of internal and external border controls of the member states, to put an end to the mass immigration it is experiencing along its coasts or land borders. the schengen computer system will always be a useless gadget as long as the dangerous schengen agreements exist.
in writing. europe wants to protect itself against shipping accidents and pollution of its seas and oceans. we welcome that. the recent tragic examples of the prestige and erika shipwrecks are a reminder of our duty to take precautions, to control the safety of ships, but also to be responsible in the event of an environmental disaster. the proposal for a directive on post-accident investigations should also be mentioned in particular. for the first time, it was agreed to set up an investigative body to decide, in an independent and impartial manner, whether to open a safety investigation to determine the causes and circumstances of an accident. the intentions are good, let us only hope that they will not remain unchanged in the face of the enormous financial interests at stake.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report by my belgian colleague, mr dirk sterckx, on the regulation of maritime traffic. since the sinking of the erika in 1999 and the prestige in 2002, we have been waiting in vain for european solutions to prevent such disasters from happening again. the risk is not diminishing, but increasing day by day: maritime traffic is expected to triple in the next thirty years. despite this alarming observation, a majority of member states did not hesitate to "leak" the main advances proposed by the european commission, and defended by the european socialists. the idea of an insurance scheme which, through a financial guarantee, was to make it easier for victims of maritime disasters to be compensated disappears. voting for this text is therefore opposing the cynicism and irresponsibility of the states. parliament can be proud of its unity, because its vote today clearly affirms its commitment to safer and less polluted european waters.

in writing. in the aftermath of the erika and prestige oil tanker disasters, the european socialists led the fight for 'high-end' maritime safety legislation in the eu. the seven reports in this 'third maritime safety package' are a decisive step towards this objective, if they are not emptied of their content by the council! since 2007 and the first reading, the council has rejected most of parliament's recommendations on the other five. for this second reading, and after intensive amendment work, parliament reaffirms its absolute priority for the establishment of a european maritime policy with a very high level of protection on: - flag state control; - the community system for monitoring maritime traffic; - the liability of passenger carriers; - inspections on ships and investigative bodies; - the designation of an independent authority responsible for ships in distress; - the application of the polluter-pays principle to the maritime sector. i strongly support this message to the council. i call on nicolas sarkozy and dominique bussereau to ensure that the french presidency establishes the birth certificate of a virtuous maritime area in europe.
in writing. i voted in favour of the trautmann report because it focuses on the social, cultural and economic value of radio frequencies and on better management of the radio spectrum for the benefit of all operators and consumers. this first reading also makes it possible to propose a balanced alternative to the european commission's initial proposal by placing the commission in the position of arbiter and not judge with regard to competition control. it is important that national regulatory authorities can continue to play their full role. i regret, however, that mrs trautmann's oral amendment was adopted. the amendment, which is apparently consensual, introduces in practice a hierarchy of fundamental rights for the benefit of end-users by prohibiting any preventive action without prior judicial notice in relation to the communication and distribution of online content. the tragedy that occurred yesterday in a finnish school and the spread of horrific images on the internet should now, more than ever, call for us to put in place reasonable and proportionate prevention mechanisms. that was the whole point of the cooperation amendment which i supported and i therefore deplore the current status quo in the european parliament.
in writing. more than 20 years after the first agreement on tropical forests was concluded, it is clear that over-exploitation and illegal logging continue. it was therefore imperative to revise the agreement to take better account of these new objectives. this is now a reality: the international tropical timber agreement, negotiated by the commission in 2006 at the un conference on trade and development (unctad), illustrates these new concerns for the sustainable and lawful exploitation of forest areas. i welcome the integration of these objectives. however, the aim is not to impose the costs which these new provisions will inevitably entail on producers in the countries concerned. the international community must therefore set up an appropriate system of financial compensation. i also hope that the commission will go further and draw up comprehensive legislation so that only timber and derived products from forests managed in a sustainable manner and harvested legally reach the european market. this is the only way to encourage producers to produce legally and in a way that respects the environment and thus to encourage the rational and sustainable exploitation of tropical forests worldwide.

president lula has just rightly and forcefully called for at the united nations. thirdly, we must break with the complacency and condescension of a small elite explaining to the citizen that there is no other choice worth making than his own. let us at least discuss all this seriously with an open mind and a great sense of responsibility. then the crisis would have been useful.

president of the council. - mr president, allow me to say a personal word, mr president, to express how pleased i was to meet my colleagues from the committee on social affairs, chairman andersson, anne van lancker, ria oomen-ruijten, jiří maštálka and many others. i would like to extend my cordial greetings to them. john bowis, for the epp, put the question in the right place, asking: 'what does europe do for me?' he raised the question of a europe of proximity and was followed by many speakers such as dagmar roth-behrendt for the socialist party and jules maaten for the alde. and finally, many participants insisted, following john bowis, that patients prevailed over states and systems. yes, of course. but this is not about ultimately pitting patients, states and health insurance systems against each other because destabilizing health insurance systems would have terrible repercussions on the organization of care and, precisely, on the patients we want to protect. that is why i will reply to dagmar roth-behrendt that the question is not about the right of patients to move within the european union, because that is obvious, that right is fundamental. the question is the one raised by the directive, the question of reimbursement and the conditions for reimbursement, the question of whether or not one is entitled to reimbursement. article 152 of the treaty is clear, states are free to organise and finance the provision of care as they wish. the central issue in the prior authorization procedure is the balance and soundness of the accounts of the solidarity and health insurance systems of the member states, especially the poorest ones. this text reminds us of this responsibility and, under no circumstances, can this directive be a means for the states to exempt themselves from these responsibilities. so, indeed, jean lambert said: 'cross-border care is not an end in itself' and derek roland clark said that perhaps we should ensure that the provisions of the new directive do not ultimately benefit only a few of the richest, best trained and best informed patients, while the imbalances would then obviously hit the poorest patients. the crucial issue, the issue which is finally being debated and which deserves to be discussed in depth between the commission and the council, is the question of prior authorization for hospital care, because this is where the greatest risks of deregulation of national systems lie. jean lambert asked whether the draft directive was compatible with the regulation on the coordination of social security. the compatibility of these two methods of reimbursement has been confirmed by the court. we must therefore ensure that these two paths are properly linked. the current draft directive gives priority to the application of the regulation, which seems reasonable. however, the patient's freedom of choice must continue to apply if, for reasons other than financial, he prefers the path opened by case law. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'common carrier' to cover all transport services, including the carriage of goods by road. when we see the difficulties that this simple text has to overcome, we imagine that having proposed such a broad text would have been the best way forward in relation to the solutions we have to consider for very concrete problems, such as the reimbursement of health care when travelling to europe for study, work or even just for holidays. in the same way, this is not a directive on health services, whether we regret it or welcome it. so there is no point in waving a so-called "bolkestein" scarecrow. that is not the subject of this directive. the directive must therefore allow us, once its fundamental principles have been reaffirmed, and i have noted them, to preserve, as is the case between the commission and the council, but also with many members of parliament in all these committees, a certain form of regulation as regards respect for these possibilities for the patient. as regards prior authorisation for cross-border healthcare, member states should remain in control of the determination of their care basket. it is equally important that the state which imposes a number of conditions on access to care for public health reasons - think for example of the referring doctor system or what is called gatekeeping in english - that these systems can be respected and implemented when one uses a health system in another country than their own. of course, this discussion on the directive should not be dissociated from the forthcoming commission communication and the proposal for a council recommendation on community action in the field of rare diseases, and i believe that it is quite possible to have these discussions head on. another topic which was raised by many members was the interoperability of health information systems. this directive can help to do so from a legal point of view. of course, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are only just beginning the dialogue, the discussion on this subject, which will have to cover such broad areas as data protection, the transparency of the systems, the scope. but, once again, since the directive affirms legal certainty, we could move forward on the road to interoperability, which does not mean uniqueness but simply harmonization and better compatibility. ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for the density and richness of the contributions which have greatly enlightened our debate.
member of the commission. − mr president, this has been a very interesting discussion. let me say that very often we hear the question: how can we bring the citizen nearer to the european union? this is one example of how we can make the citizen feel that the european union is doing something for him or her. under the present system, there are many inequalities. with the clear legal framework provided by the draft directive concerning citizens and the various issues we are trying to give clear information to the citizen about their rights and how they can exercise them. it is true that there are concerns. i listened very carefully to your concerns, and i am sure that during the course of the debate and the deliberations we shall have, we have to address these concerns so that the end result will be something which is really of benefit to the citizen. this is not a bolkestein directive ii – far from it – and we should never think that this is so. it is about patients’ rights and how to exercise those rights. we are not trying to harmonise health systems. member states can continue to exercise and regulate their health systems, and they can decide for themselves what benefits they want to offer to their citizens, and to what extent. we are not trying to encourage health tourism. we are not trying to give citizens the chance to have their faces and their bodies fixed; rather, we are trying to give citizens the right to have proper health care when they are sick and they need it. nor do we expect a big exodus of european citizens from their home state to another member state. according to the calculations and to the impact assessment that we have, only a very small percentage of citizens wish to go abroad. why? because they want to have the care that they need nearer to their families, they want to speak their own language and to be in a familiar environment. however, there are cases when they need some extra health care which their home state cannot provide. this is a right that we give them – this extra right to have an informed choice and decide for themselves where they go for their health treatment. indeed, we have had encouragement from the european court of justice to legislate. we cannot leave it all the time to the court to decide about the rights of the patient case by case. this is not just. how many european citizens can afford a lawyer and can afford to go to court? only a very few. therefore, we must offer solutions to all the patients, give them the right information and let them decide for themselves what they need. this is a time for all of us to work together – the council, the commission and members of parliament – to find the best possible solutions for patients. president of the commission. madam president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all express my appreciation of the role of the french presidency of the council. as the minister has just said, in the midst of the french presidency of the council, there was first the crisis between russia and georgia and now an unprecedented crisis, this world financial crisis. a crisis which has not its origins in europe - it has come from the other side of the atlantic - a crisis for which, in europe, we do not yet - and i emphasize 'not yet' - have the necessary rules which would allow us to have a typically european response. i am witness to the great efforts made by the french presidency and president sarkozy to find a european response to this emergency. the gravity of the financial crisis is clear to all of us and it is absolutely right that it should be at the heart of the european council meeting next week. addressing this crisis is an important test for the financial sector, for the member states, for europe and its institutions and for the international financial institutions. there is a wide variety of players involved banks and other financial institutions, supervisors, the ecb and other central banks, the national governments, the commission so we need coordination. and events are moving very quickly so we need speed. last week i called for a coordinated european response, because i am convinced that, without it, it will be much harder for europe to overcome this crisis. today i am encouraged by the determination of member states to work together, as demonstrated by the statement of the 27 leaders of the member states and myself on monday, the eurogroup and the ecofin meetings. but i am not yet satisfied we can and we must do more. in particular i urge member states to make a real effort at coordination to improve cooperation amongst themselves and with european institutions. yes, public intervention has taken place largely at national level because this is where the money and competences are. this reflects the fact that we are a union of states, not one single state, with situations different at least to a certain degree. member states' actions have in most cases been effective. but member states need to act on the basis of common principles and within a commonly agreed framework and to take into account the cross-border effects of their actions. i take this opportunity to welcome the measures announced today by the united kingdom, which are in line with the set of principles agreed yesterday at ecofin. of course, there are also many things that we are doing and still need to do at the level of the european institutions, both in the short and medium to longer term. the proposals i have in mind are concrete, practical and realistic. let me be clear: tempting as it may be, this is not the time or the place for political posturing and grandstanding, for announcing grand initiatives that have no chance of being followed through. markets would penalize this kind of behaviour immediately and the costs will be borne by economic operators and mainly by taxpayers. this is the time for ambition combined with realism and responsibility. in this context let me pay tribute to the ecb, which has shown itself an assured and effective global player, with the euro a key steadying force. the commission has played its role to the full. state aid and competition rules have been shown to be essential to give guarantees of a level playing field. the risk of action in one member state spilling over with negative consequences for another makes these rules more essential than ever. at the same time the commission has shown that it is fully capable of acting with the necessary speed and flexibility. i welcome the fact that this beneficial role of state aid rules and the way the commission is applying them is recognised in the ecofin council conclusions. the commission will shortly issue guidance setting out the broad framework within which the state aid compatibility of recapitalisation and guarantee schemes could be rapidly assessed. in the legislative area, we will come next week with two proposals. firstly to promote the convergence of deposit guarantee schemes. strengthened and more common rules here will be an important part of the exit strategy from the crisis. i am encouraged by the ecofin council, which has followed our proposal to at least double it, setting the common minimum threshold at eur 50 000, with most member states even going up to eur 100 000. secondly, we will come with a proposal to make sure that european financial institutions are not disadvantaged vis-à-vis their international competitors in terms of accounting rules and of their interpretation. last week i had a meeting with the representatives of the european banks, who were unanimous in telling me that this was a serious problem for them. the commission's role has been to promote awareness of the need to act and to create political momentum, and it seems that, now, the obstacles raised by some member states have finally disappeared. then there is the medium and longer term: the measures needed to bring stability and sustainability back into financial markets. i have said it before and i say it again: apart from liquidity, we need also to inject credibility into the current economic situation. fire-fighting is not enough. here commission work has been under way since the start of the crisis a year ago. member states need to show that we have learned the lessons needed to build the right regulatory framework to minimise the risks of crisis. progress on the ecofin road map agreed last year will need to be closely monitored. let me highlight three issues in particular. first i would like the council and parliament to give real priority to our proposal of last week on capital requirements. second, we will come next week with the proposal we announced on rating agencies. again, i know i can rely on your support to fast-track work on it. third, we will also review our december 2004 recommendation on executive pay, which was unfortunately ignored by member states or, to be fair, only one member state decided to follow to some extent the recommendations that the commission put forward in december 2004. this is a good illustration of the kind of resistance we have been facing in this area in the last few years. the last point is of a more systemic nature. we also need to have a further look at european-level supervision in the single financial market. there are more than 8 000 banks in the european union, but two thirds of total european union bank assets are held in 44 cross-border institutions. some operate in as many as 15 member states. this is the single market at work but cross-border banks have to deal with different systems of supervision in each member state, and national supervisors are not able to address the entirety of the banking activity beyond the national borders. it makes sense to remove the mismatch between a continental-scale market and national systems of supervision. when a cross-border bank is under pressure, finding quick solutions with several national supervisors in parallel is possible, as the past weeks have shown but, honestly, it is not easy. i know that we will face an uphill struggle with some member states on this. the current debates in the council on the solvency ii directive show the large degree of resistance that any attempt at improving cross-border supervision still faces. what we have proposed in solvency ii and in the capital requirements directive is the strict minimum we need. indeed, i am convinced we will have to go much further. so it is important to underline this point. when the commission speaks in favour of a common approach to supervision in europe, we do not do it because there is any agenda for grabbing more competences. we do it because there is a reality and the reality is that almost two-thirds of the banking assets in the european union already have a cross-border dimension. that means a european dimension, and we need to respond to this european dimension with a true european solution. so we need to launch a reflection process in order to build common ground. that is why i will be setting up a high-level group to look at the right architecture to ensure that financial markets are suited to the realities of the single market and that supervisors can work together to meet the challenge of cross-border banks. i am proud to announce to you today that jacques de larosière, former managing director of the imf, governor of the banque de france and president of the ebrd, has accepted my invitation to chair this group, which madam president, commissioner, the current financial crisis shows that when the problem is global, global action is needed. and this is especially true in the field of agriculture or food. that is why we have created the world trade organisation, which we agree on, which is trying to have global rules. it turns out that this is not quite working out as we would like, because we have a problem which is this: we have to reconcile two things, the necessary free trade on which everyone agrees, but the equally necessary protections. and protecting national economies or national agriculture is not synonymous with protectionism. the way we have done this for the last 60 years, since gatt, is an unbalanced way of reducing customs duties with the aim of eliminating them. it is technically difficult to reduce customs duties. the proof of this is that there are a whole series of mathematical formulas for this purpose: the south korean formula, the european formula or, the most famous, the swiss formula. it doesn't really work, because a product is not unitary. it is made up of many elements with very different rules of origin, and technically reducing customs duties is not as simple as one might think. we are therefore in a technical impasse and are trying politically, through negotiations, to break out of this impasse. but it so happens that scientists have invented a new customs technology: the technology of customs duties deductible by the exporter on the economy of the importing state. in practice, this deductible customs duty is converted into a customs credit equal to the amount of customs duty which the exporter has borne in the importing country. this customs credit has three characteristics: it is refundable, negotiable and extendable. it is refundable: when the exporter buys from the importer, he can deduct the customs duty he has paid. it is negotiable, because if the exporting company which has borne a certain amount of customs duties has nothing to buy from the importer, it trades its customs credit on the stock exchange or in a bank. and it is extendable: if we want to help developing countries, the importer can offer a customs credit amounting to more than the amount of customs duties. well, with this technique, you create a currency for international trade whose monetary mass is equal to the amount of existing customs duties. for example, the european union would offer 13 billion euros in international currency in the commercial field.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, since 2001 the developing countries have been negotiating in the wto a cycle that has been advertised as the development cycle. today, faced with a brutal and devastating food crisis, alerting the world to the urgency of finding a comprehensive and balanced long-term solution, these countries are waiting for us to give them clear answers to guarantee their food security. i would like to reiterate that if the cycle is to remain one of market access at any cost, we will not achieve our objective. we also know that the longer the development agreement is delayed, the further the prospect of achieving the millennium development goals will be, and unfortunately we are already far behind. in view of this crisis situation, we call for a political solution to the special safeguard mechanism to be found as soon as possible, in order to produce an effective tool for protecting small farmers in poor countries. this is a necessary step before we can continue negotiations on the other aspects, and i hope that the recent resumption of discussions on agriculture and nama will allow progress in this direction. i would like to end by referring to the amendments tabled to the text of the joint resolution. the pse group will of course call for a vote in favour of amendment no 2, which is absolutely essential to finally increase parliament's rights in international trade. we will also support the amendments tabled by the green group, but we cannot accept the one tabled by the epp, because we do not think it appropriate, in this resolution on multilateral negotiations, to call for the conclusion of new regional bilateral agreements, which we know are most often negotiated at the expense of the weakest.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, what is at stake in these wto negotiations? i do not believe that this is the fate, however noble these personalities, of mr mandelson or baroness ashton. i am not even sure that the main issue is the question of industrial tariffs, agricultural tariffs, market access. of course, we all want the agreement to be good, to be balanced for europe, but i think there are two main issues. the first is the preservation of a multilateral framework for trade. and we see how the absence of such a framework in another area of globalisation, that of financial markets, is costly in terms of risks for the economy, for the people and for our societies. and that is what is at stake, because if these six years of negotiations fail, we know that bilateral agreements will gradually replace the wto. it's an imperfect setting. we want to reform the wto - we say in our draft resolution - we want to add a better consideration of other dimensions that are related to trade, including environmental dimensions, to deal with impacts on climate change, and social standards. this is absolutely fundamental. however, it is not by dissolving the multilateral framework, but by strengthening it, that we will succeed in better organising this aspect of globalisation. the second issue - in writing. this parliament believes in the inherent beneficence of financial markets, their capacity for resilience and self-regulation, provided that there is a minimum of uniform rules at european and perhaps global level. but the current crisis proves just the opposite. it is financial disintermediation, the global european integration of the financial sector, the free movement of capital, the financialization of the global economy, the mad game of the market which creates ever more complex products, ever more disconnected from real economic activity, that have led us to the abyss. it is the nation that is protective and it is the decisions of the states that matter in the present context. the system of so-called free international competition has reached its limits and must be changed. first of all, the european union itself, whose policies and ideological orientations are partly responsible for the situation. it is now proving to be totally useless, since it is the states that act and react. it will prove its ability to cause harm tomorrow, since it reserves the right to sanction national safeguard measures in the name of competition. yes, it's time to put an end to this europe.
in writing. i voted in favour of the own-initiative report by my dutch colleagues ieke van den burg and daniel daianu from romania, which contains recommendations to the commission on the follow-up to the future structure of financial supervision. i support the formal request to the commission to make legislative proposals to improve the regulatory framework for financial services in europe not only because of the financial crisis but because we cannot build a european internal market without a european regulatory policy. i regret that the report does not ask the commission to initiate the procedure provided for in article 105 (6) of the treaty establishing the european community for suggesting to the council that the european central bank be given a mandate on the prudential policies of credit institutions. i am very much in favour of regulations which will strengthen and clarify the status and responsibilities of the level 3 lamfalussy committees (cesr for securities, ceiops for insurance and pensions and cebs for banks), by giving them a legal status appropriate to their functions.
